orc_page.lead_sub: Using waste heat to produce hot water or space heating is already common. Less common is utilizing waste heat to generate electricity. If your operation has sufficient waste heat with a temperature above 80°C, it can be processed using an ORC device, delivering ecological, economical, green electricity. Elvosolar a.s. offers turnkey solutions implementing E-Rational ORC units with electrical outputs ranging from 55 kW to 1000 kW.
orc_page.more_info_p1: ORC (Organic Rankine Cycle) is a technology that generates electricity from waste heat in the form of hot water, steam, or flue gases. While working on a similar principle to steam turbines, it differs in the utilization of organic working fluid. In this case, R245Fa refrigerant is used, which vaporizes at temperatures lower than the boiling point of water. E-Rational ORC units process low to medium-potential heat within the range of 80°C to 150°C.
orc_page.more_info_p2: Waste heat obtained, for example, from the cooling circuit of a cogeneration unit, transfers its energy through a plate heat exchanger to the working fluid of the ORC unit. The heated fluid changes its phase to high-pressure vapor. Saturated vapor then enters the expander, which spins under steam energy. The expander rotates an asynchronous generator, producing electricity and feeding it directly to the power grid. From the expander, low-pressure vapor goes to the condenser, where it liquefies again. The liquid is then pumped back to the heat exchanger, closing the loop.
orc_page.more_info_p3: The ORC unit produces electricity from waste heat while enabling a reduction in emergency cooling load (or disabling emergency coolers altogether, keeping them active only for emergency maintenance shutdown modes). This lowers costs in two ways - by generating clean electricity and by reducing the energy consumed by coolers and cooling loop pumps.
orc_page.ref_desc: ORC technology represents an ecological and simple way of generating electricity from waste heat. An attractive ROI provides an ideal path to lower the energy demands of industrial and utility plants.
orc_page.types_subtitle: Installed capacity outputs depend on the parameters of the processed heat (temperature and volume of available heat).
